packs.title: Kubernetes Debugging Interview Pack
packs.focus: Service routing, rollouts, Pods, probes, requests, and safe kubectl evidence collection.

questions.question: A Service returns 503 after a label cleanup. Walk me through your diagnosis.
questions.scenario: A deployment is running, the Service exists, and users get intermittent 503s.
answer_outline: Read the Service selector and namespace first.
List Pods with labels and compare selector keys exactly.
Inspect EndpointSlices for ready addresses and readiness failures.
Trace the source manifest or Helm values so the fix is durable.
strong_signals: Keeps fix in source of truth
questions.practice_task: Use the trace-service-to-pod lab and write a four-command evidence note.

questions.question: A rollout is stuck with unavailable replicas. Which objects do you inspect?
questions.scenario: A new Deployment image was merged but rollout status never completes.
answer_outline: Inspect Deployment desired, updated, available, and unavailable counts.
Compare old and new ReplicaSets and their Pod status.
Describe failing Pods for events, probes, image pull, config, and scheduling.
Use rollout history for release context and decide rollback limits.
red_flags: Confuses Service routing with rollout health
questions.practice_task: Create a rollout triage template with status, events, owner, and rollback decision.

questions.question: How do readiness, liveness, and startup probes differ operationally?
questions.scenario: A slow-starting app restarts repeatedly after probe settings changed.
answer_outline: Readiness decides whether the Pod receives traffic.
Liveness decides whether kubelet restarts the container.
Startup delays liveness/readiness pressure while slow apps initialize.
A bad liveness probe can amplify a dependency issue into a restart storm.
strong_signals: Uses traffic gate vs restart gate
questions.practice_task: Write probe review criteria for an HTTP API and a worker process.

questions.question: A Pod is Pending. What are the highest-value signals?
questions.scenario: A release creates Pods that never start, and the team suspects a cluster outage.
answer_outline: Describe the Pod and read scheduler events.
Check requests against node allocatable capacity.
Inspect taints, tolerations, node selectors, affinity, and PVC binding.
Separate scheduling failure from image pull or CNI allocation failure.
red_flags: Uses logs for a container that never started
questions.practice_task: Create a Pending Pod checklist that maps event messages to likely owners.

questions.question: What evidence do you collect before restarting a failing workload?
questions.scenario: On-call wants to restart checkout during an incident.
answer_outline: Capture describe output, recent logs, previous logs, and sorted events.
Record current rollout revision, owner, and affected namespace.
Decide whether restart is mitigation, evidence loss, or both.
Document what should become an alert, dashboard, or automation.
questions.practice_task: Write a restart decision runbook for CrashLoopBackOff.

questions.question: A Pod gets AccessDenied from AWS after a service account change. How do you debug?
questions.scenario: The same code worked yesterday, but now AWS SDK calls fail in production.
answer_outline: Identify the actual principal with SDK logs, CloudTrail, or sts get-caller-identity where safe.
Check service account, annotation or Pod Identity association, and Pod spec serviceAccountName.
Review trust policy, OIDC or Pod Identity setup, action, resource, and conditions.
Separate trust failure from permission-policy denial.
questions.practice_task: Write an AccessDenied decision tree from Pod to IAM policy.

questions.question: Why avoid broad node instance profile permissions for Pods?
questions.scenario: A legacy cluster gives every workload the node role because it is simpler.
answer_outline: Any compromised Pod may reach node credentials if IMDS is not restricted.
Least privilege requires mapping permissions to specific service accounts.
Auditability improves when each workload has its own role association.
Controllers and apps should have distinct roles and blast radius.
questions.practice_task: Review a node role and propose a migration to workload identity.

questions.question: How do you review an AWS controller IAM policy before production?
questions.scenario: A team wants to install ExternalDNS or AWS Load Balancer Controller.
answer_outline: Identify required AWS APIs and resources for the controller.
Scope resources by ARN, tags, hosted zones, cluster name, and conditions where possible.
Review Kubernetes service account, trust policy, and namespace.
Add monitoring for high-risk API activity and ownership.
red_flags: Accepts cluster-admin plus broad AWS admin
questions.practice_task: Create a policy review note for a load balancer controller.

questions.question: Explain allow, explicit deny, conditions, and permission boundaries in IAM.
questions.scenario: A role has an Allow but still cannot perform the action.
answer_outline: Evaluate identity, resource, session, boundary, SCP, and explicit deny layers.
Explicit deny wins over allow.
Conditions can make an allow apply only for matching context.
Boundaries and SCPs can cap what identity policies allow.
red_flags: Looks only at one inline policy
questions.practice_task: Annotate a denied CloudTrail event with each policy layer to check.

questions.question: How do EKS Pod Identity and IRSA change operations?
questions.scenario: An organization is deciding between workload identity patterns.
answer_outline: Both scope AWS permissions to Kubernetes service accounts.
IRSA uses the cluster OIDC provider and role trust subjects.
EKS Pod Identity uses associations and a node agent, reducing OIDC provider operations.
Both still require least-privilege policies, IMDS awareness, and SDK compatibility.
red_flags: Says identity solves all Pod isolation

questions.question: How do you choose an SLI for an API?
questions.scenario: A checkout API has many internal metrics but no user-facing reliability objective.
answer_outline: Start with user-visible behavior: availability, latency, correctness, or freshness.

Tie dashboards and alerts to the SLO and error budget.

questions.question: What makes an alert page-worthy?
questions.scenario: On-call receives noisy alerts for CPU, restarts, and queue length.

Use tickets or dashboards for slow, non-urgent operational work.
Include runbook, severity, owner, and evidence link.
Review alerts after incidents and remove noise.

questions.question: Explain burn-rate alerting in practical terms.
questions.scenario: A service is consuming error budget faster than expected.
answer_outline: Burn rate compares current error consumption to the allowed budget over a window.
Fast burns page quickly; slow burns create lower-urgency work.
Multi-window alerts reduce noise and catch sustained harm.
The alert should point to symptom dashboard and first mitigation choices.
questions.practice_task: Write a burn-rate alert explanation for a product manager.

questions.question: What should a Kubernetes incident runbook contain?
questions.scenario: Checkout latency page fires and a new responder opens the runbook.

questions.question: An ALB has unhealthy targets after a deploy. What do you inspect?
questions.scenario: Traffic fails through the load balancer, but Pods look mostly healthy.
answer_outline: Check target group health reason, listener rule, path, port, protocol, and security groups.
Compare ALB health check path with Service, Ingress, readiness probe, and app route.
Inspect subnet/AZ target registration and controller events if Kubernetes owns the ALB.
Validate from both AWS target health and Kubernetes endpoint readiness.
questions.practice_task: Create an ALB unhealthy-target checklist with AWS and Kubernetes evidence.

questions.question: Explain private subnet egress to a developer.
questions.scenario: A workload in a private subnet cannot call an external API.
answer_outline: Explain route table, NAT gateway or egress path, security group, NACL, DNS, and endpoint policies.
Check whether failure is DNS, routing, firewall, TLS, or application timeout.
Use flow logs or controlled tests when available.
Discuss cost and resilience tradeoffs of NAT per AZ versus shared egress.
red_flags: Says private subnet has no internet by magic
questions.practice_task: Draw private subnet egress and name one command or console signal per hop.

questions.question: What CloudWatch alarms would you page on for a production API?
questions.scenario: The team has CPU alarms but misses user-visible outages.
answer_outline: Start with availability, latency, error rate, saturation, and dependency symptoms.
Use dimensions and thresholds that reflect service ownership and impact.
Route urgent actionable symptoms to page; slower risks to tickets.
Link alarms to dashboards, runbooks, and mitigation choices.
questions.practice_task: Rewrite three CloudWatch alarms into page, ticket, or dashboard categories.

questions.question: How do you investigate intermittent DNS issues in AWS?
questions.scenario: Some clients intermittently resolve the wrong endpoint or fail to resolve at all.
answer_outline: Check hosted zone, record type, TTL, health checks, resolver path, split-horizon assumptions, and recent changes.
Compare results from affected networks and known-good networks.
Look for caching, propagation, conditional forwarding, and private hosted-zone associations.
Document whether the failure is resolution, routing, or application health.
questions.practice_task: Write a Route 53 triage note with record, TTL, resolver, and affected clients.

questions.question: How do you review backup and restore readiness?
questions.scenario: A team says backups are enabled but has never restored.
answer_outline: Ask for RPO, RTO, backup scope, retention, encryption, access, and cross-account or cross-region needs.
Verify restore procedure, owner, test cadence, and dependency ordering.
Check monitoring for backup failures and storage cost growth.
Treat untested backups as assumptions, not guarantees.
questions.practice_task: Create a restore-readiness checklist for a database-backed service.

questions.question: How do you reason about autoscaling in AWS and Kubernetes together?
questions.scenario: An API scales Pods but still runs out of capacity during traffic spikes.
answer_outline: Separate workload autoscaling, node capacity, load balancer behavior, quotas, and downstream dependencies.
Check HPA metrics, requests, cluster autoscaler or Karpenter behavior, node launch time, and warm capacity.
Account for cooldowns, scale-from-zero, image pull time, and readiness delay.
Use load tests and SLO signals to set guardrails.
questions.practice_task: Write a scale-out timeline from request spike to ready Pods and healthy targets.

questions.question: What does Well-Architected thinking add to day-to-day operations?
questions.scenario: The team treats architecture reviews as paperwork.
answer_outline: Use pillars as prompts for reliability, security, operational excellence, cost, performance, and sustainability tradeoffs.
Turn review findings into backlog, owner, risk, and revisit date.
Connect architecture decisions to incidents and operational metrics.
Keep reviews lightweight enough to influence real changes.
questions.practice_task: Convert one readiness gap into a Well-Architected-style action item.

questions.question: How do you debug AWS quota or throttling issues?
questions.scenario: A deployment or autoscaling event fails intermittently during peak load.
answer_outline: Identify API, region, account, service quota, throttling error, and retry behavior.
Check CloudTrail, CloudWatch metrics, service quota dashboards, and controller logs.
Decide whether to request quota increase, reduce API pressure, batch changes, or redesign.
Add monitoring so quota headroom is visible before incidents.
questions.practice_task: Create a quota headroom review for EKS node scaling and load balancer provisioning.

questions.question: What portfolio proof would you show for AWS Operations?
questions.scenario: You need to convince a hiring manager that your AWS Operations knowledge is applied, not tutorial-only.
answer_outline: Pick one artifact tied to AWS Core Operations Interview Pack: lab note, diagram, runbook, Terraform plan review, dashboard, or incident write-up.
Explain the problem, constraints, commands or design choices, and validation evidence.
Name what would change in a real production environment.
Link the artifact back to Amazon CloudWatch User Guide and the related course platform-eks-operations.
questions.practice_task: Create a portfolio README section proving one AWS Operations skill with screenshot-safe evidence.

questions.question: How would you build a seven-day crash plan for AWS Operations interviews?
questions.scenario: You have interviews soon and must turn AWS Operations gaps into answerable scenarios quickly.
answer_outline: Day 1: scan official docs and write the top concepts in operational language.
Days 2-3: complete the related lab and produce an evidence note.
Days 4-5: answer scenario questions aloud and repair weak answers.
Days 6-7: create one portfolio artifact and one STAR story tied to this domain.
questions.practice_task: Turn this AWS Operations pack into a seven-day study checklist with daily outputs.

questions.question: How do you answer when an interviewer challenges your AWS Operations recommendation?
questions.scenario: The interviewer pushes back to see whether you can reason under pressure.
answer_outline: Restate the goal, constraints, and risk the recommendation addresses.
Offer alternatives and tradeoffs rather than defending one answer emotionally.
Name the evidence that would change your decision.
Show willingness to adapt while protecting reliability, security, and user impact.
questions.practice_task: Write two alternative answers for a controversial AWS Operations decision.

questions.question: What are the common false positives or misleading signals in AWS Operations?
questions.scenario: The interview tests whether you can avoid fixing the loudest symptom in AWS Operations.
answer_outline: Name one signal that is useful but easy to over-interpret.
Pair it with a second signal that confirms or disproves the hypothesis.
Explain the safest next read-only check before mutation.
Close with the owner boundary and escalation path if evidence points elsewhere.
questions.practice_task: Add a false-positive section to your AWS Operations troubleshooting notes.

packs.title: Observability and Telemetry Design Interview Pack
packs.focus: Metrics, logs, traces, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, CloudWatch, cardinality, dashboards, and actionable alert design.

questions.question: Design observability for a new checkout service.
questions.scenario: A team has logs but no useful dashboards or alerts.
answer_outline: Start with user journeys, SLIs, and critical dependencies.
Define metrics for rate, errors, duration, saturation, and business outcomes.
Add structured logs and traces for request path and dependency timing.
Create dashboards and alerts with owners, runbooks, and review cadence.
questions.practice_task: Create an observability launch checklist for checkout.

questions.question: When do metrics, logs, and traces each change your next action?
questions.scenario: An interviewer asks for practical signal selection.
answer_outline: Use metrics to detect aggregate symptoms and trends.
Use logs for discrete events, errors, and contextual facts.
Use traces for request path, latency breakdown, and dependency calls.
Combine signals around a hypothesis instead of browsing dashboards randomly.
questions.practice_task: Write one latency investigation using one metric, one log query, and one trace.

questions.question: How do you control metric cardinality?
questions.scenario: A Prometheus bill and query latency spike after a new deployment.
answer_outline: Identify labels with unbounded values such as user id, request id, path parameters, or pod churn.
Separate useful aggregation labels from high-cardinality debugging detail.
Move per-request detail to logs or traces when appropriate.
Add metric review and instrumentation ownership.
questions.practice_task: Review five metric labels and classify safe, risky, or remove.

questions.question: How do you design tracing for a microservice path?
questions.scenario: Checkout calls payment, inventory, fraud, and shipping services.
answer_outline: Propagate trace context across ingress, services, queues, and outbound calls.
Name spans consistently and attach useful attributes without sensitive data.
Decide sampling strategy based on traffic, incident needs, and cost.
Use traces to explain latency breakdown and dependency errors.
questions.practice_task: Sketch a trace for checkout and identify the spans you need during an incident.

questions.question: How do you make dashboards useful during incidents?
questions.scenario: Responders say the dashboard has too many panels and no clear story.
answer_outline: Start with symptom panels tied to SLOs and user impact.
Group by service, dependency, saturation, recent deploy, and mitigation signal.
Add links to logs, traces, runbooks, deploys, and owners.
Remove vanity panels that do not change decisions.
questions.practice_task: Redesign one dashboard into symptom, cause, and mitigation sections.

questions.question: How do you handle observability for batch jobs and queues?
questions.scenario: A nightly job failure causes stale data but no request errors.
answer_outline: Define freshness, backlog age, successful completion, failure rate, and processing latency.
Page only when user impact or business deadline is threatened.
Add runbook steps for retry, replay, and data validation.
Track dependency and downstream impact.
questions.practice_task: Create an alert policy for a four-hour batch job with a ten-hour freshness threshold.

questions.question: How do you migrate from vendor-specific telemetry to OpenTelemetry?
questions.scenario: A company wants portability without breaking current dashboards.
answer_outline: Inventory current metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and owners.
Introduce OpenTelemetry instrumentation and collector pipeline gradually.
Preserve semantic meaning, cardinality controls, and alert compatibility.
Run dual-write or comparison periods before cutting over.
questions.practice_task: Write a migration plan for one service from vendor SDK to OpenTelemetry.

questions.question: How do you test whether monitoring itself works?
questions.scenario: The team missed an outage because alerts never reached on-call.
answer_outline: Add blackbox checks, synthetic alerts, Alertmanager route tests, and notification audits.
Monitor collector, Prometheus, CloudWatch, and dashboard pipeline health.
Practice alert delivery in game days.
Document failure modes and backup communication paths.
questions.practice_task: Create a metamonitoring checklist from scrape target to pager notification.

packs.title: Terraform Live Plan Review Interview Pack
packs.focus: Live IaC review: state, modules, plans, unknowns, replacements, drift, imports, policy checks, and safe applies.

questions.question: Walk me through your first two minutes with a Terraform plan.
questions.scenario: The interviewer hands you a large plan and asks whether it is safe.
answer_outline: Confirm workspace, backend, variables, provider, environment, and change context.
Scan summary for create, update, replace, destroy, unknown, and sensitive values.
Prioritize IAM, network, data, capacity, and deletion risks.
State approve/block/needs-evidence with validation and rollback notes.
questions.practice_task: Practice a two-minute spoken plan scan using risk buckets.

questions.question: How do unknown values affect plan review?
questions.scenario: A plan has many attributes known after apply.
answer_outline: Identify whether unknowns are harmless computed values or decision-critical values.
Look for unknowns that affect IAM, routes, security groups, replacements, or dependencies.
Use data sources, outputs, preconditions, or staged applies cautiously when needed.
Avoid approving if the unknown hides blast radius.
questions.practice_task: Mark unknown plan values as safe, needs evidence, or blocker.

questions.question: When would you use import, moved blocks, or state surgery?
questions.scenario: Infrastructure exists outside Terraform and the team wants it under code.
answer_outline: Prefer declarative import and moved blocks where supported.
Back up state, lock state, and review addresses before any state operation.
Avoid changing real infrastructure accidentally during adoption.
Document owner, source of truth, and rollback path.
questions.practice_task: Write a safe import checklist for an existing security group.

questions.question: How do you review Terraform changes from a security perspective?
questions.scenario: A plan changes IAM policies, security groups, and KMS access.
answer_outline: Identify new principals, actions, resources, conditions, and trust relationships.
Check ingress, egress, public exposure, encryption, and logging changes.
Look for wildcard permissions and broad CIDRs.
Use policy-as-code or review templates for repeatable checks.
questions.practice_task: Create a Terraform security-review rubric for IAM and security groups.

questions.question: How do you structure Terraform environments for promotion?
questions.scenario: Dev, stage, and prod drift because engineers copy-pasted stacks.
answer_outline: Use shared modules with versioned releases and environment-specific inputs.
Separate state per environment with clear backend and workspace rules.
Promote module versions intentionally through environments.
Review differences as configuration choices, not accidental drift.
questions.practice_task: Design a dev-to-prod promotion flow for an EKS module.

questions.question: What should policy-as-code catch before apply?
questions.scenario: The organization wants guardrails without blocking every useful change.
answer_outline: Catch high-risk patterns: public ingress, unencrypted storage, missing tags, broad IAM, and destructive changes.
Separate warnings from hard blocks.
Allow documented exceptions with owner and expiry.
Keep policies understandable to the engineers they affect.
questions.practice_task: Write five policy checks for EKS infrastructure plans.

questions.question: How do you handle a failed apply?
questions.scenario: Terraform partially applied changes and then failed while updating node groups.
answer_outline: Stop and inspect state, real infrastructure, error, and what completed.
Avoid rerunning blindly until drift and partial changes are understood.
Decide whether to fix config, import/update state, roll forward, or roll back.
Communicate impact, owner, and next validation step.
questions.practice_task: Write a failed-apply recovery note with state, live resources, and next action.

questions.question: How do you explain Terraform risk to a non-IaC interviewer?
questions.scenario: A manager asks why plan review takes time when automation exists.
answer_outline: Explain that Terraform automates changes to real infrastructure, including network, IAM, and data paths.
Use blast radius, rollback difficulty, and state as plain-language concepts.
Give examples of safe quick changes versus changes needing review.
Connect review quality to incident prevention.

packs.title: Kubernetes Platform System Design Drill Pack
packs.focus: System design interviews for Kubernetes platforms: multi-tenancy, release paths, observability, cost, upgrade strategy, and developer experience.

questions.question: Design a Kubernetes platform for 30 product teams.
questions.scenario: The interviewer wants architecture, operating model, and tradeoffs.
answer_outline: Clarify team needs, service criticality, compliance boundaries, and cloud constraints.
Choose cluster strategy, tenant boundaries, networking, identity, delivery, observability, and support model.
Define golden path defaults plus exception process.
Measure reliability, cost, adoption, lead time, and security posture.
questions.practice_task: Draw a platform architecture with tenant, control-plane, data-plane, and ownership boundaries.

questions.question: How would you design namespace onboarding?
questions.scenario: A team needs self-service access without waiting on platform tickets.
answer_outline: Generate namespace, RBAC, quotas, NetworkPolicy, cost labels, dashboards, alerts, and ArgoCD app scaffold.
Require owner, service tier, data classification, and support model.
Use policy checks and templates for safe defaults.
Expose exceptions as reviewed, expiring records.
questions.practice_task: Write an onboarding template for a new team namespace.

questions.question: How do you design upgrade strategy for shared clusters?
questions.scenario: Multiple teams deploy CRDs, webhooks, and Helm charts into shared production clusters.
answer_outline: Inventory APIs, CRDs, webhooks, clients, add-ons, and tenant manifests.
Provide compatibility windows, test clusters, dry-run checks, and owner deadlines.
Sequence control plane, add-ons, nodes, and workloads.
Publish pause criteria, rollback limits, and communication plan.
questions.practice_task: Create an upgrade program plan with tenant checklist and dates.

questions.question: How do you choose between one shared cluster and many clusters?
questions.scenario: Security and cost teams disagree on platform topology.
answer_outline: Compare isolation, blast radius, compliance, cost, operational complexity, and team autonomy.
Use separate clusters for hard isolation, high-risk workloads, or regulatory boundaries.
Use shared clusters when guardrails and support model are mature enough.
Document tradeoffs and migration path.
questions.practice_task: Write a decision record for shared versus dedicated clusters.

questions.question: How do you design platform observability as a product capability?
questions.scenario: Every team builds dashboards differently and incidents are slow.
answer_outline: Provide default RED/USE dashboards, log/tracing standards, alert templates, and ownership labels.
Let teams extend views while preserving core SLO and incident surfaces.
Integrate deploy events, runbooks, and service catalog metadata.
Measure adoption and incident usefulness.
questions.practice_task: Design a standard observability package for new services.

questions.question: How would you make cost visible without blocking delivery?
questions.scenario: Teams over-request resources and finance wants controls.
answer_outline: Add cost labels, namespace reports, request/usage views, and service-owner showback.
Set sane defaults and recommendations in templates.
Create review workflows for extreme requests or expensive resources.
Tie cost changes to reliability and product context.
questions.practice_task: Create a monthly platform cost review format for service owners.

questions.question: How do you design break-glass access?
questions.scenario: Normal access is least privilege, but incidents sometimes need emergency power.
answer_outline: Define who can request, approve, assume, audit, and revoke emergency access.
Make access time-bound, logged, ticket-linked, and reviewed after use.
Keep normal workflows least privilege so break-glass is exceptional.
Test the process before an actual incident.
questions.practice_task: Write a break-glass access runbook for production Kubernetes.

questions.question: How do you handle platform deprecation?
questions.scenario: The team needs to retire an old chart, runner, or cluster version that many services still use.
answer_outline: Inventory consumers, risk, replacement path, deadlines, and support burden.
Provide migration tooling, docs, office hours, and compatibility checks.
Communicate with enough lead time and escalation path.
Track adoption and exceptions until the old path is actually gone.
questions.practice_task: Create a deprecation plan for an old Helm chart or Kubernetes version.
